lines: A spreadsheet is a grid of cells. Columns have letters, rows have numbers, so column B, row one, is cell B1. Excel and Google Sheets are the ones you'll use.

A formula always starts with an equals sign. Put your forty dollar price in B1 and twenty five tune-ups in B2. In B3, type equals B1 times B2, and it shows one thousand dollars. Change B2, and B3 updates by itself.
Functions are ready-made formulas. SUM of B2 to B4 adds twenty, twenty five and thirty, for seventy five. AVERAGE gives seventy five over three, or twenty five a month.

When you copy a formula down, its cell addresses move with it. To lock a cell, like your price, add dollar signs: dollar B dollar one always means B1. Forget them, and the copy points at an empty cell and shows zero.

A model keeps every input in its own cell, in blue, and everything else is formulas. Never type a number into a formula. With five more tune-ups each month, six-month profit is four thousand fifty dollars. Change that one input to ten, and it jumps to six thousand three hundred.

Excel's NPV function treats every cash flow as arriving at the end of a year. So for the repair van, NPV of the five three thousand dollar years gives eleven thousand three hundred seventy two dollars. Subtract the ten thousand you pay today outside it, and you get one thousand three hundred seventy two.
Finally, always check one row by hand. If January's profit matches, twenty times thirty dollars minus three hundred, or three hundred dollars, the copied formulas are right too.
